speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. On July 13, 1976 in Hansard at page 15286 the former minister of public works said that no agreement had been signed with the Campeau Corporation concerning Les Terrasses de la Chaudiere project in Hull, Quebec.
In view of the fact that the Campeau Corporation under date of June 28, 1976 had an information circular in the hands of certain financial houses in Canada for the purpose of raising $148,500,000 and also the fact that only eight days after the minister's statement in this House the Department of Public Works had signed extensive documents of lease with the Campeau Corporation, and because the terms of the documents indicate a financing factor of approximately $50 million more than a reasonable estimate of cost for the area leased by the government, I move, seconded by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens):
That all further progress on construction and financial arrangements cease until all matters pertaining to possible conflict of interest and the apparent excesses involved in the financial arrangements have been examined by a judicial inquiry.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to direct a question to the President of the Treasury Board. Given the fact that the state of the government's management and controls systems is significantly below acceptable standards of quality and effectiveness and the fact that the Auditor General, in testimony before the public accounts committee, revealed that unless the systems are corrected the day may very well come when a clear certificate of the accounts of Canada cannot be given, may I ask the

October 19, 1976
President of the Treasury Board when he will be in a position to present to parliament an up to date progress report on the implementation of the recommendations of the Auditor General, as was agreed to in committee, in order that we might restore some confidence in the government's ability to manage and control the financial affairs of this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: PROPOSED CHANGES IN ACCOUNTING METHODS AND FORM OF PRESENTING ESTIMATES-REQUEST FOR PROGRESS REPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there has been some discussion of this matter between myself and the Auditor General and I consider it to have been very helpful and constructive. As to the precise date when I will be able to do what the hon. member suggests, I can only say that it will be at the first possible opportunity. I want a little more time to digest some of the details, although I am aware of the need to move on this. Indeed, some action has been taken already with the appointment and establishment of a deputy secretary within the Treasury Board secretariat with the precise responsibility of monitoring and expanding financial controls and financial management, which is a step in the direction of the recommendation of the Auditor General. I share the hon. member's concern and I want to get at it as quickly as possible.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED CHANGES IN ACCOUNTING METHODS AND FORM OF PRESENTING ESTIMATES-REQUEST FOR PROGRESS REPORT
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Dealing specifically with the form and content of the estimates, might I ask the President of the Treasury Board whether the review has been completed, whether changes are contemplated and, if so, whether such changes will be incorporated in the estimates of the next fiscal year. Might I also ask the President of the Treasury Board whether he will be asking members of parliament for their suggestions and input regarding the form and content of the estimates. I ask this particularly because it is members of parliament who are charged with the task of scrutinizing and examining the estimates.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and is further to the minister's statement to the press in Washington last Friday. Will he inform the House if the proposed transition fund agreed to between himself and Dr. Kissinger is intended to help Rhodesia and her government improve her economic status, or is it to be used mainly for the purpose of helping white Rhodesians leave their country to settle in other countries including Canada?

October 19, 1976
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: RHODESIA-PURPOSE OF PROPOSED TRANSITION FUND-SUGGESTED PARLIAMENTARY APPROVAL BEFORE PARTICIPATION IN FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to be able to answer the question. Before doing so I should emphasize, however, that there was no agreement with regard to this matter between Canada and the United States, for the simple reason that Secretary Kissinger indicated they were not ready as yet to indicate in detail what kind of proposal they were making. He made it clear that he would hope for Canadian participation in the fund.
As to the substance of the hon. member's question, as I understood it from Mr. Kissinger the objective of the fund is to stabilize or to help stabilize the economy of Rhodesia, and also to discourage a mass exodus, I think was the word I used at the press conference in this regard, of white Rhodesians following the establishment of a majority government in that country. In other words, the fund would be weighted, as it was explained to me, in favour of those who are going to remain in Rhodesia, or who are prepared to remain there and carry on their normal activities.

subsubtopic: RHODESIA-PURPOSE OF PROPOSED TRANSITION FUND-SUGGESTED PARLIAMENTARY APPROVAL BEFORE PARTICIPATION IN FUND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since there was no agreement, will the minister assure this House that before any specific commitment is made by Canada in this regard parliament will have an opportunity to debate the whole matter, preferably by way of a resolution introduced by the government in this House?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: RHODESIA-PURPOSE OF PROPOSED TRANSITION FUND-SUGGESTED PARLIAMENTARY APPROVAL BEFORE PARTICIPATION IN FUND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not know what is the appropriate technique, but I can certainly assure the hon. member that, in so far as I personally am concerned, I would be very glad to make available to the House, or to do it publicly, whatever proposals are put forward and to provide an opportunity to discuss them. I emphasize that this is premature at the moment because nothing has been transmitted between us other than the explanation the secretary gave me during my visit.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to take advantage of this occasion to make a brief statement. It is a matter of personal privilege for me to say that I am resigning my seat in this House effective midnight tonight in order to contest a seat in the legislature in my home province of Prince Edward Island, where I have been chosen provincial leader of the Progressive Conservative Party.
Hear, hear!

While 1 consider my new responsibilities a great challenge, it is naturally not without regrets that I leave this chamber after 25 years' service. I will especially miss the honour of representing the people of the constituency of Malpeque, some of whom were also members of my former constituency of Queen's. They have done me the honour of electing me ten consecutive times to this chamber, thus making me their representative in one third of the parliaments elected since Confederation.
Hear, hear!

I would like to record my deep appreciation to you, Mr. Speaker, and to all the members and staff of this House for the many courtesies extended to me on so many occasions. I will miss the many friendships I have been fortunate to enjoy among you.
I will, of course, miss working in the parliamentary associations in which I have been active, and I will miss my work as chairman of the Standing Committee on Management and Members Services and the close association this entailed with the Commissioners of Internal Economy.
Whatever the future holds, I hope I may be able to retain at least most of the friendships I have enjoyed here. Let me wish you all continuing good health and satisfaction in your respective responsibilities to our country.
Hear, hear!

As a minister he performed exceedingly well, and following his departure from the ministry he has served as a member of the opposition, on committees and in the House of Commons in an extremely effective way. However, I believe all of us will remember Angus MacLean mostly for his personal qualities, his readiness to extend friendship and his high integrity.
He is leaving the House to take on new responsibilities, and judging from recent events he does not require good wishes from me in order to discharge those responsibilities.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my colleagues in the House I would like to join with the government House leader in extending our very warmest personal wishes to the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. MacLean). As the government House leader has said, during his 25 years in the House the hon. member has distinguished himself as one of the truly exceptional gentlemen of this House, and that is said in the most positive sense. He is a man of honesty, integrity and personal commitment to the wellbeing of his constituents.
In expressing wishes for continuing good health and personal happiness to the hon. member in the most genuine fashion on behalf of my colleagues I, of course, want to make it abundantly clear that we do not extend these good wishes into the political domain. I am sure the hon. member understands that. We wish him well as he returns to his native island. We hope the political success he confronts there is not at all commensurate with the 100 per cent personal success we wish him.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to join in with the two previous speakers, on behalf of the Social Credit Party of Canada, to congratulate the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. MacLean) for the beautiful speech he made last night. In the person of the hon. member for Malpeque, Mr. J. Angus MacLean, the House of Commons loses an extraordinary man, an every day man of duty and also a man respected by all. I know he will surely fulfill other as honourable functions and that he will be as devoted as he was in the House of Commons. Our wishes of success and good health be with him.

I hope hon. members will permit me to just add a word if I may. Not much can be added to the wonderful tributes that have been paid so deservedly to the Hon. Angus MacLean. May I only say that the Management and Members Services Committee is a recent addition to the roster of standing committees of the House and the work of that committee provides a service which potentially benefits or should benefit all members of the House. It benefits the Speaker of the House directly in the difficult decisions of attempting to strike a proper balance between those services which members require to fulfil their obligations and those which they deserve in terms of the financial burden of the estimates of the House.
For that committee to reach its maximum potential it really required in its infancy a chairman who ought probably to have come from the opposition side or at least have been able to demonstrate a very objective point of view, one who could bring to that post many years of experience both in and out of cabinet as well as a reputation for objective judgment and the respect of all of his colleagues. At the same time, that person should enjoy a reputation for a sane and sensible hand on the throttle.
I think we have all been deeply fortunate that we found such a chairman in the Hon. Angus MacLean. I wish to express my appreciation and that, I know, of all members for this latter aspect of a career which has been a great donation to the House of Commons.

Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) during his very able and eloquent address; namely, that members of the Liberal Party do not have to conduct a post mortem as to the reasons for what happened. I was interested in the questions asked earlier this morning concerning secrecy. Mr. Speaker, the government opposite has an all-time record for concealment and equivocation. Although there is incorporated in the Speech from the Throne one of those generalizations concerning the expectation of the possibility of a hope for a change, I see not that repentance which should be evidenced by the government following the Rudnicki case. At one time those high in the echelons of the public service were servants of the people. They used to sign their

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker letters, "I have the honour to be, Sir, your obedient servant." They do not do it any more. They do not tell the people that they want to be their everlasting masters. That attitude was revealed in the Rudnicki case. Somebody took a document and stamped it confidential. Why, if all the papers marked confidential by the present government were not to be seen by those outside the cabinet who have eyes to see, there would be a great reduction in the amount of paper work in this country.
I recall being bitterly condemned by those who were then in opposition for having produced a document which the Department of Trade and Commerce, under the St. Laurent administration, had hidden. It contained information showing how seriously the economic conditions of Canada were being undermined. I did not get the document from the department: a member of the press handed it to me. The Prime Minister described his government as a "government of the middle". There is a mistake. One vowel is wrong. It should be "government of the muddle". I occupy an objective position today. I hold no position in my party and I am therefore able to weigh governments of today against those which preceded mine. I have never seen a government so accident prone. If they don't get one, they create one. No one can deny that this is an absent-minded government. The more I watch it in action the more I believe the Prime Minister meant what he said-one time-when, asked what politician or political writer had guided him the most, he uttered the immortal words: The one I particularly admire is Machiavelli. All I can tell you is that Machiavelli said in effect: Fool people, deceive them, and then, from time to time, give them little gifts; but pursue your course and do not object to untruths. That is what Machiavelli said almost 500 years ago. But it is surely not a proposition to be accepted today. I am not going to discuss financial matters.

I was there. I was received most hospitably by the Prime Minister of Japan who became a close friend of mine and gave me his most valuable picture in the room where he had me sit with his cabinet. And the Emperor and Empress had Olive and me to lunch. I do not wish to digress but I always recall a story which indicates the sense of humour of the Empress. It had been reported that I was fond of hunting and the Emperor said to me through an interpreter: "We are going to take you hunting." I said: "What kind of guns do you use-what gauge?" He said: "We don't use guns, we use a net and as the ducks come in we pick them off along the canal." I said: "That looks all right to me. What kind of ducks?" "All kinds", said the Empress. "Mallards?" "Oh, yes." "Greenheads?" "No," said the Empress, "they are redheads; they originate in Siberia." Mr. Speaker, anyone with a sense of humour like that is worthy of being quoted.
I do not intend to deal with inflation except to say to the House that when I was prime minister we had the lowest rate of inflation in all the world-1.1 per cent. My authority for this is the former President Kennedy of the United States who was never one of my particular friends. One of the reasons was this. When it became known that a corporation was going to raise the price, for instance, of bread, the head of that corporation was communicated with and an explanation sought. Increased costs, and so on, he might say. Our reply was to this effect: All right, you go ahead. But as soon as you do there will be an investigation by the Combines Investigation Branch and if you are right you will be right, but if you are wrong proceedings will be taken. Believe me, they did not raise their prices very readily, though the action taken did not make me very popular in some quarters not too far from Ottawa.
What is the government's record on inflation? They can argue about it until the end of time, but I will simply quote from the record. After nearly a year of wage and price controls which were imposed to lower inflation, is the Canadian economy more competitive than its leading rivals in the world? Not according to the International Monetary Fund. A survey on world inflation was produced by economists at Citibank of New York. These economists suggest that Canada has not benefitted as much as most other nations from the break in inflation during the past year, and that its price performance is worse than in the years 1970-1975 while several other countries are doing better than they were. Such a report cannot be denied, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, before lunch I had come to the point where I was going to deal briefly with the constitution. I will deal with it at greater length on another occasion, as I have already spoken longer than I normally do.
Our Canadian parliament is made up of the Queen, the Senate and the House of Commons. The one question that keeps recurring in my mind is why there is such an ungodly rush to patriate the constitution. Mr. King tried, Mr. St. Laurent tried, and when I was prime minister we had it except for two very small matters. We delayed for a couple of weeks and then there were objections raised on a couple of matters by the premier of Quebec and the premier of Saskatchewan. Then Mr. Pearson tried, without success.
What is the reason for this rush? Why not take a little time? Great Britain does not want the matter brought to the attention of parliament regularly when we require amendments, but we have never been able to agree as to what the terms should be. Until we do agree, what do we bring back? What will we have gained by unilateral action? The parliament of Great Britain might say that this statute is repealed, and then what will we have for a constitution? What will come back to Canada? It will all be repealed and we will have to start all over again. I do not think anybody wants that.
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker
What is behind this? 1 am not one who normally wonders about these things, but I must say that I was greatly interested in a speech delivered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on March 5, 1976, before the fifth provincial congress of the Liberal party of Canada. Let me read these words from this portion of the speech that was not distributed very widely and which has never beert referred to. Let me read it without observation in order that I may conclude at the earliest possible moment. The Prime Minister said, and I quote from page 1:
-there is the division of powers that we have not been able to solve, there is the amending formula but most important of all there is what people call repatriation; basically this means that we are going to take away from England, the United Kingdom, this foreign country although it is a friend, the right to make laws for Canadians. It should not be very hard to come to an understanding on this point.
He goes on to say, after referring to Britain in rather unusual terminology, "this foreign country":
Do you think that the Queen of England will tell Bourassa: admit that Trudeau is right or tell me, admit that Bourassa is right?
I do not know how that arose. Then he rewrites history on page 2 by saying:
Every single Commonwealth country has done it. When the Westminster statute was adopted in England in 1931 it read exactly as follows: from now on the British Empire does no longer exist in those five countries, those five Commonwealth dominions. We will no longer make laws for them.
You were colonies before but in 1931 the English said: Well, South Africa, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland and Canada are now big enough to make their own laws. Canadians said no, we are not able to.
I am interested in the fact which he points out, that after the 1931 Statute of Westminster no longer were any of the countries colonies, and they were not at that time. He says they are now dominions, which answers once and for all the argument that the word "dominion" carries with it a connotation of colonialism. He went on to say;
What we are saying is that if we should not reach agreement, let us agree that from now on the English will not have the right to make laws for Canada. But this has to be done soon.
Then he said:
What we are trying to say is: Let us reach an agreement to bring back that constitution, let us do it without discussing the division of powers; we can always argue about it later; we do not need the Queen as an arbitrator, or Harold Wilson or the Pope for that matter. We are able to do it ourselves. This is what we are saying and I am adding, what if it did not work? You will have to make a decision and I think that there is even a resolution on this point. We should, perhaps, at that point, wonder if we should not do that on our own, if it will not simply be a matter of the Canadian parliament going to tell England: Stop making laws for us; we are going to discuss an amendment formula among Canadians.
The Prime Minister continued:
And I can see it coming, not too rapidly because we must not rush people too much but when we realize that it has been discussed for 49 years, I have the impression that we must not wait for another 49 years, because I will not always be there, at least me-

Then he went on to discuss separatism. Ele pretended that the Conservatives do not agree with the government and he said:
-Or even if the Tories do not agree with us and want to guide their campaign by saying: The Liberals should have left the constitution in England, so that the British could have kept on making laws for us-
That statement is repugnant to the truth. I hope that people who want the constitution to remain in England for a time will not defeat the majority. There is no one in Canada who does not want the constitution patriated. Elowever, we still cannot agree on how it should be done. Then he said:
Now, since we are talking about England, I would like to say a few words about the Queen, as a transition, because next I would deal with the Olympic games-
Tie said he did not invite the Queen of England. Sir, let me say she is not only the Queen of England, she is the Queen of Canada.

He said he did not invite the Queen of England to open the Olympic Games; it was CO JO who invited her. In fact, it was not COJO which invited the Queen. The agreements among the various countries constituting the Olympic organization contain a provision that the head of state opens the Olympic Games, and the head of state in Canada during the Olympics was Her Majesty the Queen. Then he said:
It is not Pierre Trudeau who invited her. But I would not have been ashamed to invite the Queen, for she is the head of the country.
Now we come to the key sentence, in which he said:
If, one of these days, we abolish monarchy, she will not be the head of state any more, it will be someone else, in this case, Jules Leger, it will be someone I will appoint.
This is a very fine dissertation, and I read it to those in the Liberal party who can explain this clearly and definitely.
He said, in effect, l'etat c'est moi. Louis XIV was never more impressive than was the Prime Minister of Canada who said, "it will be someone I will appoint". He went on to say:
It does not mean, according to the present constitution that he or she will be better than the Queen, but it will be another constitution, it will not be a monarchy any more, it will be a republican parliamentary democracy-
Now you see what the rush is all about. Through the years from 1940 to 1976 his dream has been that there is something wrong with the Queen of Canada. Indeed, two years before he became Prime Minister he said, pay no attention to the Queen; she is of no more importance to me than skating or snowshoe-ing. He has never denied that since, and I said this when he was here.
Let me read further from what he said:
-and instead of having the Queen as head of state, we will have Jules Leger in Ottawa or Hughes Lapointe here-
He meant, in Quebec. Then he went on:
I do not think that it would change very much our legislative methods but I do not want to enter this subject now. I only want to state clearly that 1 am not the one who invited the Queen ... The COJO invited the Queen.

I could read a great deal more. These words cannot be interpreted in any other way but that when the constitution, or whatever remains of the BNA Act, comes to Canada, he will be in a position, not someone else, to appoint a president.

First, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that as early as next spring I intend to launch a big campaign for promoting exports across Canada. Hopefully it will be an education and information program for Canadian businessmen by the officials of my department, who are specialists in foreign trade. We hope that the best among them will be able to hold conferences across the country so that the very competent officials working abroad might educate Canadian businessmen and initiate them in foreign trade.
I think that the hon. member who has already been Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce did a somewhat similar job when his party was in power and I should like to insist on this because I think that at this time Canada has an extremely favourable potential in this area. Ours is only a small country with no extra-territorial ambition but on the other hand, we have a modern technology, which is acceptable in many countries. I must also say that, after my first contacts with the ministers who visited Ottawa since I have been here and after the tour I made in South America, I am convinced that such a program for initiating businessmen in exports will certainly be very useful and that it will have great results.
Mr. Speaker, I should also like to be particularly interested in the great projects which are being carried out in the world at the present time. When I visited Venezuela a few weeks ago, I realized that we Canadians are too often very timid when it comes to those so-called turnkey projects, that is extensive and comprehensive projects.
Too often in those projects, there is a lack of coordination and sometimes of government intervention. What is happening in today's modern world? Very often major decisions such as the great Venezuela railway or other projects of the same nature in Iran or Sandi Arabia are made by governments, and we are not adequately organized here in Canada. And if the department or even the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce does not intervene we often run the risk of missing our chance. That is why I would like to consider the possibility of establishing-and I have not yet submitted the project to Cabinet-some sort of corporation to deal with that problem and also form within the country many consortia that could really offer comprehensive projects entirely acceptable to interested countries.
There is another problem I would like to deal with, Mr. Speaker. Often in our domestic trade, businessmen do not always think in terms of the best interests of Canada and they cut their throats-if I may use that expression-in certain

countries trying to get one another out of a contract. I think it might be necessary in the future for the government to decide on its own which Canadian businessman is better equipped to do a certain job.

When I was in Venezuela I learned that Canadian technology can be applied more usefully in that country than can certain types of European technology. An example was the Venezuelan railway system. We are experts at building railways over rough terrain. We have built railways across the most difficult terrain in the world, in the Rockies, in the marshes, in the north. I'm always welcome in Alberta. My mother comes from Alberta; everybody knows that. There are some in this House who always talk about free trade, yet in the same breath they ask us to impose quotas on beef and veal. Well, we have done it. Some traders abroad were abusing our good will; we were being flooded with imports from Australia and New Zealand, and when the Americans imposed restrictions last week I had no choice but to act. As soon as we knew what the picture was, we moved very quickly. We knew there would be a price to pay. We knew we could not win on both fronts at the same time. We had to be very careful. This is a free trading nation. We export a great deal and would like to export more. At the same time, however, we have to protect Canadians in productive occupations, such as textile workers and beef producers. It is better for Canadians to continue working in the textile industry in certain areas than to remain idle. However, Canadians must realize that in order to do this we must impose a quota and therefore run the risk of some of those goods being a bit more expensive. I am willing to take that kind of risk.
If hon. members have concrete proposals and ideas, I hope they will pass them on to me. I would be delighted to listen to them. I ask hon. members on all sides of the House to help me in my new job, keeping in mind our common goal-the well-being of this nation.

speechtext:
I want to indicate that I will be moving an amendment to the Speech from the Throne at the conclusion of my remarks.
This throne speech, delivered in a most excellent and graceful manner by Canada's first lady, in complimentary terms can
October 19, 1976

only be viewed as a vague and feeble attempt to revive the increasingly sagging fortunes of this government. It attempts vainly to repair the irreparable. It sends messages off in all directions and to all regions, but fails totally to offer any concrete solutions to the problems which it addresses, problems which for the most part have been accrued, and indeed have been caused, during this government's time in office.
Given the record of this government and the current mood of Canadians, which has been mainly fostered by the performance of the government, unfortunately I have come to the conclusion that the content of the throne speech is simply meaningless. In other words, it does not matter what the government now says; people simply do not trust the words or the print of a government which has previously deceived us and has provided such ample evidence of its worth that our citizens have developed an entrenched mood of dissatisfaction and disenchantment. You cannot, under any circumstances, hope to maintain the trust of people by completely ignoring their problems and wishes, or by continuously taking the attitude that governments are always right and the people are always wrong.
This throne speech adds insult to injury with respect to the agricultural industry. Like the last budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), it deals with one small agricultural item-unbelievable and unacceptable but, given the record of this government, understandable. There is only one paragraph announcing one commitment to agriculture, namely, "Measures will be introduced to make more farm-stored crops eligible for advance payments." This legislation is not new; it was promised by the minister over a year ago. It has simply been promised again. Let us hope that it does not turn out like the other few agricultural bills-introduced, given no priority at all, and finally passed months or perhaps a year later. Other references to agriculture in the speech are simply an example of the rhetoric. One is:
The Government will also work with the provinces and farm organizations to strengthen the structure and productivity of Canadian agriculture.
In reality, this government will more than likely pretend to work with the provinces and farm organizations but will, in fact, accomplish next to nothing as it continues to mismanage the structure, to discourage productivity, to perpetrate instability and to generally shrink the scale of the agricultural industry. Farm input costs have increased so much in the last few years that credit is not only needed for long-term farm goals but is required for year to year cash flow. A few examples of these increased input costs include a rise of 47 per cent in fertilizer prices between 1975 and 1976, an increase of 17.6 per cent in building replacement costs, according to Statistics Canada, a 24.6 per cent hike in the cost of petroleum products for farm purposes, a 13 per cent rise in the cost of farm labour, and a 16.2 per cent increase in the cost of electricity.
Yet against this type of background farm credit has been reduced. The funds available to the Farm Credit Corporation in the current 1976-77 fiscal year have been reduced by the Minister of Finance from $300 million to $280 million. It is
The Address-Mr. Wise
expected that gross FCC loan commitments will only total about $370 million this year compared with $641 million in the previous fiscal period a reduction of almost 50 per cent. This situation is having a disastrous effect among young farmers who cannot obtain the required credit sources. Is this the kind of action you would expect from a government which professes to care about agriculture?
Perhaps one of the main reasons for the low priority treatment given to agriculture is the obviously declining influence and importance of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). Until fairly recently, farmers generally were pleased with the minister. Given the fact that farm income has nearly always, characteristically, lagged behind others, and given the fact that input costs have risen beyond even the wildest imagination, they rejoiced to hear the minister tell their story. It made for great entertainment in hundreds of rural community halls and secondary school auditoriums across the country. But what is the situation today? The smiles have disappeared and the laughter has faded as farmers begin to realize what has been obvious in the House of Commons for months, that the minister cannot translate his wishes into legislation, nor can the minister act when he wishes to act. I believe he has even less influence in this government than he had a year ago. The federal dairy policy, which has created more unrest, instability and financial strife within the industry than ever before, is a prime example. In spite of all opposition warnings, the minister, or rather the cabinet, overreacted to the dairy surplus problems of the past year. Surely the minister must be aware that the dairy cow cannot be turned off and on with a toggle-switch.
Deficits and surpluses have existed before and they will exist again. We are still desperately in need of a long-term program. Where do we see any mention of such a program in the Speech from the Throne? My hon. friend from Joliette (Mr. La Salle) will deal with the dairy situation in more detail later today. The minister has failed to produce any kind of program for cow-calf operations. He has refused to implement a Canadian meat import law. He has done nothing about the unfair Canada-Australia-New Zealand meat agreement. What about the report of the beef inquiry commission? When is the minister going to act or, perhaps, more realistically, when will he be allowed to act? My hon. friend from Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) will later be offering some good advice to the government on this subject.
The stabilization payments for the 1975 apple crop amounted to a clear indication of cabinet interference with major agricultural legislation since they constituted a departure from the main thrust and intent of existing law. Because of the total failure of federal policies we are now seeing massive intervention programs by the provinces to bail out their own producers; for example, the recent program in Saskatchewan, at a cost of $30 million, and the program announced not too long ago by the Province of Alberta for a cow-calf program to which the provincial government had to contribute some $40 million.

October 19, 1976
The Address-Mr. Wise
Witness, too, the Quebec dairy subsidy of $33 million. The question of federal and provincial jurisdiction has arisen and we may soon face yet another jurisdictional clash. The provinces, however, are acting only to protect their own industries from almost certain ruin. The very fact that these programs have become necessary amounts to the ultimate condemnation of abortive federal policies.
I have made statements before in the House on the subject of federal income tax and the capital gains tax as they relate to farm ownership and farm transfers, but as yet I have received no significant response either from the Minister of Finance or from the Minister of Agriculture. Present federal regulations clearly discriminate against the transfer of family-owned farms incorporated or organized in partnership, or other kinds of family organizations. Since this discrimination seriously threatens the transfer of such farms to succeeding generations, I propose that the rules governing such transfers be the same, regardless of the type of organization, as long as the farms are family-owned.
As has been previously stated both by myself and by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the government should also consider the exemption from capital gains tax of the income received by a farmer or family-owned corporation where the money is invested in another farm within two years. This would allow a farmer, if the need arose, to buy one farm and sell another for the sake of a more efficient operation. Similarly, moneys from all forced sales should be given at least a two-year exemption provided they are reinvested in the industry. The utter disregard shown by the government for proposals in favour of reforms such as these has clearly demonstrated to Canadian farmers that the federal administration cares little for them and their needs. Small wonder that the popularity of hon. members opposite has fallen so low.
Over the past few months we have heard rumblings about a comprehensive new food policy for Canada. It was indicated in the Ottawa Journal of May 8-and this has been verified in ensuing investigations-that the key department in the development of such a policy is not the Department of Agriculture but the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Mr. Speaker, this situation is totally unacceptable. It is an insult to the Department of Agriculture and to the industry generally. If Canada needs a new food policy, its proper place of origin and development is within the Department of Agriculture, though let us, by all means, take account of input from all sources, particularly those representing the consumer.
The present and future livelihood of producers is totally dependent upon an equitable policy, and in these circumstances their advice and counsel on any such venture is imperative, particularly when it comes through their respective commodity groups. When we hear that policy papers have already been prepared for cabinet consideration, I fear for the future of agriculture, especially in view of the government's past record of secrecy and deliberate confrontation. We in the official opposition are working hard to overcome the distrust which has been built up, largely because of the actions of the government, between producer and consumer groups. We will

not subscribe to proposals which will pit producers and consumers against each other. There has been too much of that. The present government has set a bad example. We intend to set a good one when we on this side come to power.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity to interject a few words on behalf of the maple sugar and syrup production industry, most of which is centred in the province of Quebec.

speechtext: Don't forget Parry Sound.

speechtext:
I shall not forget Parry Sound-Muskoka. One could perhaps forget the riding, but never the member who represents it. In spite of the fact that many countries show a keen interest in importing this sweetener, production has declined by almost 50 per cent in the province of Quebec during the last 20 years. Increased prices have been insufficient to provide healthy revenues to existing producers or attract newcomers to the long-time tradition. Maple syrup production in 1975 was about 1.3 million gallons, 21.7 per cent less than in 1974 and 950,000 gallons less than during the years 1956-60. I hope I can prevail upon the government to check this decline and save this traditional and valuable industry. I would be very interested to hear what the government intends to do regarding this vital matter.
The pork producers, as represented by the Canadian Pork Council, constitute another group within the agricultural sector which remains unimpressed by government performance. They are still very upset over the tariff cuts on pork announced last May by the Minister of Finance in his last budget. I might say that the importation of pork and pork products increased by 110 per cent in 1975 as compared with 1973. Mr. Elder, president of the Canadian Pork Council, has been quoted as saying:
Our pork prices are now set on a North American market basis. The cutting of tariffs as proposed will simply put an additional downward pressure on Canadian pork prices and further shake the confidence of Canadian hog producers, many of whom are currently considering whether to increase, or even continue in production. Producers with the support of a number of provincial governments are currently working in many ways, and at considerable expense through stabilization and marketing schemes to increase production following the recent production decline.
He went on to say that this cutting of tariffs will be interpreted by many producers as a further indication that the federal government is not concerned about the development and stability of the industry.
During the past two years I have spoken out on many occasions on dairy policy, particularly on the question of cheese imports into Canada. On this particular issue agriculture has been fighting a losing battle with industry, trade and commerce and likely the trend will continue. It is interesting to note, with all of the chaos and unrest that exists in the dairy industry today, particularly among the industrial milk producers in the province of Quebec, that statistics indicate that importations of dairy products have increased some 83 per cent in 1975 compared with 1973. This is only one example,
October 19, 1976

however, of increased strife within the agricultural industry caused by ever-increasing amounts of agricultural products.
Let me take a look for a moment at the Statistics Canada figures on imports; I have them before me and 1 also have the percentage increases in 1975 compared with 1973. Berries, 370 per cent; apples, 58 per cent; honey, 211 per cent; jams, 74 per cent; chicken, 289 per cent; canned hams, 33 per cent. I think the largest and most significant percentage increase of an imported product is tobacco. The subject of tobacco is not only very close to my heart, because I have a large acreage in the riding of Elgin, but I know my colleague who represents the riding of Norfolk-Haldimand (Mr. Knowles) is also extremely interested in this product. The increase in tobacco imports in 1975 compared with 1973 is a whoopping 1,086 per cent.
It is obvious that some restrictions, or at the very least increased tariffs, are required. Instead, the government is removing tariffs, such as that on sugar. This effectively removes any possibility of the revival of the sugar beet industry in southwestern Ontario. I regret that the Minister of Agriculture is not here because I would have been very interested to hear his comments regarding the removal of the tariff on sugar. I wonder whether he supports this measure, particularly when he has campaigned election after election on the promise to re-establish the sugar beet industry in southwestern Ontario.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: He only does that at election time.

speechtext:
That is true. Two production areas that are being adversely affected by the import situation are those of chickens and soybean production. In 1974, total importations of U.S. chickens into Canada amounted to approximately five million pounds, or less than one-tenth of one per cent of Canadian production at that time. In the same year, Canada exported to Cuba nearly 12 million pounds of Canadian-produced chicken. By 1975, imports of U.S. chicken had escalated to over 12 million pounds, and with literally no export of Canadian chicken this represented an increase of 250 per cent. Up to June, 1976, U.S. imports of chicken continued to swell and now total 22 million pounds, live and dressed. This in just under six months. At this rate, Mr. Speaker, imports may reach 50 million pounds this year, an increase of over 400 per cent compared with 1975, and represents 7 per cent of our total Canadian production. Since the vast majority comes into the province of Ontario, this represents 25 per cent of Ontario's total production and is ever increasing. Chicken producers are not happy with this situation, but to date the government has turned a deaf ear to their protests and representations.
Producers of broiler chickens are equally concerned about the increased importation of American broiler chickens. It has cut into the production quotas of Ontario broiler producers who were hoping to get back to regularity after having quotas reduced last year to 85 per cent of capacity in order to avoid a surplus or overproduction. There is a further danger, of course, that the broiler producer will be forced to accept a reduced return because of the necessity of cutting prices in order to
The Address-Mr. Wise
compete with American imports, which due to climatic and other conditions can be produced at less cost, generally speaking at about 25 per cent less. This unfair competition is a serious threat to the Canadian broiler producer.
Soybean growers, too, are now facing the prospect of reduced returns for their product as a result of unchecked foreign competition. Mr. Otis McGregor, chairman of the Ontario Soybean Growers Marketing Board, said recently that producers can expect to receive substantially less for this year's crop. Much of this reduction is due to increased competition from the United States, which exported 2.2 million bushels of whole soybeans to Canada during the previous year in addition to soybean meal, oil and flour, for a total market value of $145.8 million. Canadian exports for the same period amounted to only $15.1 million.
A familiar and disturbing pattern is now obvious, one of increasing agricultural imports and decreasing exports. Tariff barriers are established by our competitors to hinder the export sale of our products, yet imports continue to flow at alarmingly unchecked rates into Canada. Our producers are not being adequately protected. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) is doing farm producers and the agricultural industry a disservice by allowing this situation to continue unchecked. The Minister of Agriculture is losing all credibility by failing to bring any significant influence to bear upon the government's position.
We know that farmers want to produce, Mr. Speaker, and they should be given every opportunity to do so with as little government interference as possible. By and large, producers will adjust and adapt to changing market conditions. Canadian producers welcome competition and can compete in any marketplace given similar circumstances. But Canadian producers cannot, and should not, be expected to compete in the marketplace against heavily subsidized foreign products and commodities. Farmers should be assisted by government to seek out and develop foreign markets. At the same time, farmers should be called upon to develop more aggressive sales programs, both here at home and abroad, for their produce. The quality of Canadian food production is the highest in the world and can fulfil, with no problem whatever, any advertising or promotion program.
Were some reference to any of the matters to which I have spoken included or even vaguely mentioned in the throne speech, Mr. Speaker, I might have been able to find some sign of hope or encouragement from the pronouncement. But, as usual, the agricultural industry has been completely ignored by this insensitive and unthinking government. From the point of view of the agricultural community and of those dedicated to serving its interest, this throne speech is totally devoid of merit.
As I indicated when I began my remarks some time ago, Mr. Speaker, I feel a definite desire, indeed obligation, to submit the following motion, which is seconded by my colleague from Joliette:
That the following be added to the Address:

October 19, 1976
The Address-Mr. Saltsman
"This House regrets that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to support the productive sectors of the economy, and in particular have not responded adequately to agricultural problems such as the distress of the industrial milk producers, the excessive importation of beef from Australia and New Zealand, and the lack of effective co-ordination between federal and provincial agricultural authorities.

Mr. Speaker, I should like, first, in my opening remarks to congratulate the new Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) and wish him well. He is going to need all the good wishes we can offer if he is to do anything with his new department. I do not say that because I have less than considerable respect for the personnel of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. In the years I have been here, I have had many occasions to consult and work with officials of that department regarding various constituency problems, and I have always found the personnel most helpful and, in fact, a very able group.
The problem is not the result of the personnel or the department itself but, rather, because the department has to serve a government that has no conception of any industrial strategy or policy. The result is that the department has become kind of an Augean stable of the kind that even Hercules, like the present minister, was not able to clean up. Some of you may remember the story about the Augean stables which Hercules laboured day and night to clean, only to find the next day that it was just as filthy.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It was Ulysses.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Well, the minister doesn't look very much like Ulysses.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It doesn't matter, you are shovelling the same stuff over there anyway.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
You are experts over there, so I am sure you have the right handle on it. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, for all his apparent enthusiasm for some of the ideas he intends to put forward and changes he intends to make in the department, will really wind up doing what previous ministers of trade and commerce on that side of the House have been doing for as long as I have been here, and that is jawboning. He thinks he can jawbone the department and its policies into success. It is quite obvious that as his hero the minister has picked the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees), particularly as an example of effective jawboning, when that member held the portfolio in the Conservative government. The difficulty is, of course, that the present minister does not have the same effective jaw as the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings and should not, therefore, try to compete in that league.
If we consider some of the things the minister said in his remarks today, we must ask ourselves whether he really understands anything at all about his job and the problem facing him. First of all, he starts out talking about facing some

problems. Certainly that has to be the understatement of the century in terms of the problem facing this country today.
Let me put on record the kind of position we find ourselves in at the present time. Between 1968 and 1974 Canada experienced the lowest rate of growth in the volume of exports of any major non-communist, industrial nation. The latest 1975 figures have been excluded from this comparison since they are heavily influenced by the world's cyclical contraction. Over that period real exports rose by an average annual rate of 5.7 per cent in Canada, 8.8 per cent in the United States, 12.1 per cent in France, 13.5 per cent in Japan, and 7.1 per cent in Britain. Even in beleaguered Britain it rose 2 per cent more than it did in Canada. Moreover, only two other industrial countries aside from Canada saw the volume of their imports expand more rapidly than their exports. Over this period real economic trade trends were worse for Canada than they were for Britain.
Canada's trade balance, measured in terms of stages of fabrication, has over the past decade continued to shift in a direction politically unpopular at home. The merchandise trade surplus has expanded continuously in crude materials and fabricated materials. However, in the fully-finished end products sector-that is where the jobs are; the sector which accomplishes the bulk of manufacturing-the reverse has been the case. Canada's merchandise trade deficit on end products has widened in every year since 1968. Part of this deterioration may be traced to an adverse movement in auto trade, though growing deficits have emerged in other finished products as well. Even excluding the eight most important export commodities, Canada's trade balance in the remaining products has displayed a similar deterioration since 1968.
The point of some of these figures which I have gone over quickly is that we probably have demonstrated the worst expansion, in terms of trade among manufacturing or developed nations, in the world. We must ask ourselves how a country with the resources of Canada and with the people here could do so badly in trade. The minister summed this up by saying we are facing "some problems". When it came to solutions, the minister suggested he would welcome ideas from anyone. I suggest he will need ideas from someone else because he will not get them from that side of the House.
The Minister takes considerable pride in the fact that the government has appointed a Minister of State for Small Business. I do not oppose this; I think it is very nice to attempt to help small business, at least to the extent possible. That still does not deal with the central problem relating to our trade deficit. At best it is window-dressing, if you will, or public relations. Small business, like motherhood, is something that no one is against.
The government will not create jobs, in the kind of world in which we live, by assisting small business. Small business in many cases can perform valuable functions that often big business cannot perform. Those of us who know something about small business will know that these businesses are often heavily dependent on giant industry. Small businesses are not initiators, innovators or creators of the large number of jobs
October 19, 1976

we require. They are ancillary and very important, and should be encouraged, but I think it would be like burying your head in the sand to think you can create the number of jobs this country requires by stimulating small business. I think every country in the world has demonstrated the fact that we live in a world in which we must have large industry. We must have large industry in order to be able to carry out research and marketing as well as the many other things associated with being internationally competitive.
We have some fair-sized industries in this country, but we have never quite developed the coherent or comprehensive kind of Canadian industrial structure to cause a presence in international competition. This is partly because of the presence of foreign ownership.
It is interesting to note that, as hard as those responsible for FIRA have tried, we have not been able to reverse this trend of foreign ownership by getting more Canadian businesses going when others are put up for sale. That organization has attempted to transfer ownership from foreign corporations to Canadian corporations. In spite of the good intentions of FIRA, the fact is that when you get down to it, for some reason Canadians have not been in a position to take over these businesses when they have been put on the market.
There have been some successes where Canadians have participated in the take-over of foreign corporations, but they have often occurred as a result of the government intervening and supporting the take-over and transfer of ownership. It is difficult to understand why Canadian entrepreneurs are in such a weak position and why the risk-taking that is occurring in other countries is not occurring here. Perhaps if we look back at our history we will find we have never had that kind of capitalistic society in Canada and that in fact Canadian entrepreneurs, with few exceptions, have been timid and heavily dependent on government.
Many projects in this country might never have got off the ground had it not been for public involvement or the government stepping in and, in fact, assuming the bulk of the risk. What does that say for us? I suggest it says that unless we can change the Canadian entrepreneur and the financial institutions, then the government of this country will have to play a much larger role in the development of industrial production. That is the way it has been done in the past, and that is the way it will be done in the future unless the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce adopts an attitude different from that of the ministers before him, an attitude of wringing their hands.
We can dissipate these problems by jawboning, by going out and assaulting the markets of the world as though we were the only ones who wanted to go out and assault the markets of the world. You must have something to offer the markets of the world, and the truth of the matter is that we are not in a position to do that. All the super-salesmanship in the world will not change that.
The Address-Mr. Saltsman
Whenever we talk about our being uncompetitive, the only ting that comes to some people's minds is that wage rates in Canada are too high. There are many other reasons why we are competitive and why our productivity is not high. One is the way our industries are organized and the way they compete or do not compete with each other. Productivity is not so much a matter of the guy who works at the lathe; it is a factor of industrial organization. We are not as productive as we should be, and we have to be productive. How are we going to be productive? Hon. friends on my right are listening with some interest and 1 am pleased to see that. One of them seems to be on the verge of standing up and making a suggestion. Perhaps he would like to say that the way to increase productivity is to get the government's cotton-picking hands out of the pockets of Canadians and away from businessmen who will show you how to be productive.
I see by the glint in his eye that that is the argument he was about to put forward. I wanted to save the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) the trouble of exercising himself to rise and ask a question, so I asked it in a rhetorical sense. I say to him: Is it really true? Because in fact this government has been more generous in terms of tax benefits than almost any other government I can think of. What more do businessmen in Canada want? They get low rates of taxation. The effective rate of taxation in this country is not that high or that devastating. This is not the reason people cannot compete.
I have had some experience, as have my colleagues in the House, trying to find a group of Canadian businessmen who are prepared to take the gamble of trying to persuade the banks of this country to stick their necks out. Unless it is a safe risk, with guarantees right down the line, you do not have that group of indigenous Canadian capitalists to do the job. Perhaps we will develop them some day; I do not know. But we do not have them now, and the truth is that we have not had them, with a few exceptions such as the E. P. Taylors and the Lord Beaverbrooks. To show you what Canadian ethics are, we drove them out of the country. We could not tolerate the likes of Lord Thomson.

speechtext: You contributed your share to that.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I did not. In fact, 1 made a speech in the House in praise of Lord Thomson, if not for his tendency to accumulate money, at least for his integrity in admitting that that was the sole purpose of his endeavours. The man is gone now, but I have no animosity for Lord Thomson. As a matter of fact, I found him to be a rather nice fellow on those occasions when we met in London; so let that be on the record.
I think we are in the kind of position where jawboning, exhortations and launching assaults on foreign markets will not do any good. The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is indulging itself in a fantasy. The truth of the matter is that the minister, whatever his good intentions may have been today in putting forward this program and speaking of the kind of things he is going to do, in fact does not have the power to do them. The reason he does not have the power to do them is that the government is without a policy, without a
222

October 19, 1976
The Address-Mr. Saltsman
strategy, nothing is co-ordinated, everything is ad hoc. If you are going to make your economy competitive, you have to take a systematic look at all the factors that enter into being competitive, the factors that enter into the reasons you cannot trade and others can.
I was curious to know what the minister meant when he spoke about the export business and said that very often in export contracts Canadian businessmen compete for a job, and that that is very bad. I always thought the Liberal party thought competing for a job was a good thing. Now they are saying that when you do it on export contracts, it is a bad thing. Therefore, he as minister, and presumably his government, will have to decide which business is best for the job, to quote him exactly. If there is an overseas job to be done, instead of having a number of Canadian companies competing for the job, the minister will make a decision and say, "We think A should go rather than B".
As I sat in my place listening to the minister, I kept trying to figure out exactly how he is going to go about doing that. Is he going to sit down with them in his office and review the kinds of bids they are making, and say to them, "Look, fellows, you really should get together. Your bid should go, but the other two should not". If that is the case, I am sure the combines people would be very interested in such conversations, even though consortiums for export purposes are exempt from the provisions of the combines legislation.
If we are going to bring people together on that basis, and if the minister really thinks he can get them to collude and combine for export purposes and there will not be some kind of carryover arrangement for the domestic market, that is the company turns out to be reasonably successful in selling on the export market-I do not think it will be, but at least successful to the point that it will get a higher price than it might otherwise obtain-will there not be a spillover? Will someone not come to the conclusion that if it works there, why should it not work in the domestic market? I think they came to that conclusion a long time ago. The minister underestimates the amount of collaboration that takes place in domestic and foreign markets.
What is there about the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce that makes it so ineffective? I have pointed out in my remarks that I think they have some excellent people. My experience with the department has been good. When I come to them with a problem, I find people who understand, and more than understand. They are willing to really move on the thing. It is not often you can call a deputy minister on a Sunday and get some action from him, or have civil servants working halfway through the night on a deal because they know it is urgent and important. But that does not seem to be the problem. The problem is that the rest of the government's policies make it impossible for the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce to be other than the Augean stable to which I referred. It is just a stable where they throw all the junk, saying that they have to try to compensate for all the disastrous policies they have in other areas and come up with some money to bail out an industry here, make a grant

somewhere else, and do all those things which make up for the deficiencies in the policies of the government.
Let us consider some of the things which happen in this country. First, the government-and not only this government but also governments before it-can never make up its mind whether it has to concentrate on the manufacturing industry, agriculture or the resource industry. Perhaps governments have not wanted to make up their minds because that would have involved making a value judgment or decision. Governments have never really done that. They say they will concentrate on everything, manufacturing, resource industries, agriculture and fishing. They want to please everybody, and let the investment go where it pleases.
There have never been any conscious investment policies. What is the effect of that? The effect is that Canada is a very attractive resource country, and if investment in Canada is left alone, by and large the bulk of that investment will go to the development of resources. That is a natural thing, particularly when many investors are foreigners, with plants in other countries, who are looking for iron ore, asbestos or other raw materials to satisfy the needs of their manufacturing facilities. That is what has happened.
The consequence of this large influx of investment has been to raise the value of the Canadian dollar. The raising of the value of the Canadian dollar and the maintenance of high interest rates which accompany that-and sometimes interest rates are used to stimulate investment coming in-has virtually killed the manufacturing industry. It makes imports cheaper, and exports dearer. Even if our productivity were as good as that of every other country, this policy of maintaining a high value on the Canadian dollar would be disastrous enough. However, when our productivity is not as great as that of other countries, the consequence of maintaining the Canadian dollar at a higher level than the value of our chief competitor, the United States, for example, is virtually to ensure the destruction, or certainly the crippling, of the manufacturing industry in this country.
Our dollar is based on productivity and, after all, that is what a floating exchange rate is supposed to do. A floating exchange rate is supposed to reflect the differences in productivity between one country and another, and on that basis our dollar should be in the region of 90 cents to 94 cents to the American dollar, certainly not at a premium to the American dollar.
The hon. member who preceded me pointed out some of the difficulties with which he is familiar in the agricultural sector, and what has been happening to some agricultural producers. Surely part of the problem, in terms of what he was describing from his experience, also arises from the high value of the dollar. Whether we talk about chickens or machinery, it is the same kind of thing. If our dollar is higher than the American dollar, it is cheaper to go to the United States and buy chickens there. Certainly the Americans will not buy chickens from us, all other things being equal, if our dollar is more
October 19, 1976

expensive, if they have to pay more for it or if their currency does not buy as much in Canada. Yet the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is expected somehow or another to go out and sell Canadian products and have nothing done about the value of the Canadian dollar. That is an impossible thing to do. Little wonder they have to go back to the stable the next day and find it just as full as the day they left it. We have this kind of policy.
The Minister referred to his concern for the unemployed, and I am sure his concern is genuine. But how is he going to achieve full employment in Canada, with the kind of policies this government has been creating? He made one reference which I thought deserved at least a tag line or a credit line for the NDP. He said something along these lines, "We did not go into a recession. We have done better than other people." In my view, the only thing that saved this country from one of the most serious recessions we have ever had-certainly, one which would have been more serious than in the United States-was the fact that over the years the NDP has had some influence in forcing some welfare policies on the government. Without those support programs in this country, without unemployment insurance, without the various grants which are available, and without old age pensions, we would have been so flat that we would have made the thirties look like a picnic. Those are the only things that saved the government-not its cleverness and not its policies.
It is the fact that we have instituted support programs which maintain purchasing power when the inadequacies of the government show and it is not able to do anything about developing an industrial strategy and creating jobs. Unfortunately, while that prevents some of the worst hardships falling on people, it is not what this country wants. The people of this country want jobs. The result of operating these kinds of policies is that we have perhaps avoided a desperate recession, but at what a cost! We have spent money on unemployment insurance and on welfare policies, and lost dignity in many cases. All this could have been avoided by the creation of jobs and the adoption of adequate policies.
One has to ask why, in the face of close to one million unemployed in this country, the government maintains two measures which by everyone's judgment contribute to the loss of exports and the diminution of jobs. The two measures I refer to are high interest rates and the high valuation of the Canadian dollar, which are government policies. Those things do not happen by accident; the government wants it that way. Why does the government do this? I presume it is because it has come to the conclusion that we might have a little more inflation than we have now if we were to move the other way; in other words, in order to have full employment we might have extra inflation. However, now that this whole business of inflation has-become less of a real issue than it has become a political issue, the government has brought in its measures under the Anti-Inflation Act. It is quite clear that the AntiInflation Board has had a very minor effect, if there has been an effect at all, on prices in the industrial sector.
The Address-Mr. Saltsman
The figures which show that our inflation has decreased are related to what is happening internationally, but more particularly they are related to some stabilization in the price of energy and a very considerable drop in the price of food. Those are the significant factors in the drop in the increase in the cost of living. If we move away from high interest rates and from a high valuation of the Canadian dollar, one of the initial consequences, because we import so much from the United States, will probably be to raise some prices in this country. I say some prices, but in my view, if it is done in a determined and phased way it should not have any significant inflationary effects. However, we have a government which is scared and whose whole life, if it still exists, seems to hang on success in demonstrating that it has licked inflation or brought it down significantly.
This government is terrified to make any kind of trade-off in favour of creating employment in this country, getting jobs for people or improving our export potential, because these things might show up as a percentage point on the inflationary scale. They have tied their success so much to the Anti-Inflation Board that they are willing to jeopardize every other policy in order to make it look good. I think it is disastrous for this country.

I do not pretend, and 1 am sure no other member of the House pretends, to possess the kind of expertise that the minister may have in his department. But what we do have is a kind of overview, and ability to look at what is happening over there. It is our job to be critical, to try to understand what is happening-because everyone is deeply concerned over what I think is a disastrous record in terms of job creation in this country.
There may come a time when we do not have to worry about job creation. It is said that in the 1980s the big boom will be over and then we can turn to capital-intensive industries. At the moment, however, this generation needs jobs-now. At the same time, the government has to make a deliberate choice with regard to creating those jobs. It is going to cost us in some other areas; it may mean that some large resource developments may have to be deferred. So be it, if that is what has to be done.

The greatest service the minister can offer in his new capacity is to bang the table in the cabinet room and say that his department cannot operate unless it gets some kind of plan, some kind of industrial strategy, some kind of industrial outlook which puts all the policies together in such a way as to improve our competitive position.
