speechtext:
It is really a pleasure to take part in the debate this afternoon. The Speech from the Throne and the legislation to be enacted in this session of the thirtieth parliament will, to be quite candid, make or break the Liberal party, the party I represent, the government I have supported for two years and the government I will continue to support.
There has been much rhetoric in this debate concerning the evils of inflation, the anti-inflation program, the problems of implementation of the Official Languages Act, the continuing energy crisis and countless other problems that afflict Canada. In my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I would like briefly to lay before the House the facts as they pertain to the economy and then relate those facts to the political climate which I believe has caused a great amount of uncertainty within the country.
It will be my contention, Mr. Speaker, that the basic problems facing Canada are not overly economic, not necessarily social, not even necessarily linguistic, not cultural, but political. I shall fly a trial balloon for restructuring the parliamentary system as we know it, then conclude with some remarks on the question of national unity and bilingualism.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, let us take a quick look at the economic situation. With the introduction of the anti-inflation program, the inflationary psychology which gained significant momentum in late 1974 and 1975 has, at last, been broken and therefore one can say the policy has been a success. There are those on the other side, especially members of the New Democratic Party, who contend that the anti-inflation program has not been successful in bringing down the rate of inflation but, rather, the huge slide in food prices has been the main reason for a drop in the consumer price index from over 10 per cent to a 6'/2 per cent annual rate, based on the August figures.
These critics argue that food prices do not fall within the purview of the anti-inflation program and, therefore, the program has had little real effect on the inflationary rate. This is false, since transportation and distribution costs, which do fall under the program, are built into the cost of food products at the retail level.
I think the main success of the program so far has been, as I mentioned earlier, the breaking of the anti-inflation psycholo-
[Mr. Saltsman.J
gy. The exorbitant wage demands that we saw manifesting themselves over the summer of 1975 have, of course, been drastically affected by the program. These labour costs would have worked their way through the pricing system and resulted in huge price increases in 1976. As a result, the rate of increase of retail prices has been significantly curtailed, but not enough, Mr. Speaker, for us to say that the program should be abandoned at this particular time.
The Prime Minister talks about continuation of the antiinflation program until 1978. I am not so sure that we can wait that long, because the main advantage of any statutory program of wage and price controls is its immediate shock value and as the program bites into more and more sectors of the economy and into personal incomes its popularity diminishes. In addition, any protracted period of controls will drastically restrict business expansion. The program should be wound down over the summer of 1977.
I think it is fair to say, Mr. Speaker, that over the past two or three years, when every industrialized country in the world has been beset with the problems of rapid inflation and high unemployment, Canada has weathered the storm as well as any other nation, with the possible exceptions of West Germany, Sweden and Norway. It is true the economy has not grown. It is true that Canadians, for the first time since the depression, have seen their living standard remain at a standstill. But there has been no decline in the standard of living in this country such as that which has been witnessed in Great Britain, France, Italy and Japan.
Economic recovery is under way and I have no doubt that within two or three years, as the Speech from the Throne indicates, Canada will once again achieve prosperity, although the rate of growth of Canadian prosperity will in no way match the doubling of disposable incomes that we have seen in the past 20 years. Those days, I believe, Mr. Speaker, are gone forever. However, the Canadian people should be told that there is hope for a more gradual betterment of their life in both a material and a spiritual sense. This is borne out by the economic projections we have before us, not only from domestic bodies such as the Economic Council of Canada but also from external agencies such as the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development.
While the standard of living in this country has been marginally affected by inflation and unemployment, we have seen the terrible eruption of many social problems and a trend toward general disrespect for the traditional values and institutions of Canadian society. I think it is not an exaggeration to say that there is great hostility in the land. Much of this hostility is directed toward government at all levels but, of course, is more noticeable in the hostility toward the federal government and the leader of that government who is our Prime Minister.
This is something of which we on this side of the House are fully cognizant. Liberals are engaged in an exercise of searching among ourselves and among our ideas so as to put into proper context the degree of criticism that faces the Prime Minister and the government. We are trying rationally to analyse the reasons for the government's unpopularity and to bring forth concrete policies which respond to the concerns and the frustrations of Canadians.
October 19, 1976

It appears, Mr. Speaker, that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) does not have the inclination nor perhaps, if the truth be known, the ability to apply himself rationally to the issues which are causing disquiet among Canadians. As we saw in one of the most cliche-ridden and transparent speeches this House has heard from a party leader, certainly in my two years here and perhaps a lot longer than that, the Leader of the Opposition shows a complete lack of insight as to the forces which make this country tick. He talked of Canada as being, and I quote:
-above all, a partnership and the essence of a partnership in this country is to establish a basis of mutual respect and trust. That is broken down in Canada. It is not an accident that it is broken down. It is not due to impersonal forces from abroad, it is broken down because of now nearly a decade of the practice of this government of taking unpredicted unilateral actions and unilateral decisions.
How facile! What rubbish!

But it results not from the unilateral actions of the Liberal government; rather, it is, 1 believe, due to the failure of the parliamentary system as we know it in this country to operate effectively.

Not only is mutual respect and trust breaking down but, indeed, I believe the country is in danger of breaking up. It is breaking up because this House is not truly a representative one. The concept of a representative parliament on the British model has served this country well for 100 years. But the pace of social and economic change and the regional diversities of the country have led to a situation where parliament, this body of which we are all honourable members, no longer reflects the will of the people.
We, as Liberals, have argued with some pride that we have been the one and only national party in this country. It has been clear for a long time, and I believe the Prime Minister gave official recognition to this point in his speech in Toronto a few weeks ago, that our party can no longer make that claim. Our condition in western Canada is feeble-that is being polite.
By the same token, the Progressive Conservative party is Still principally an English-speaking party with scant representation from the province of Quebec and, in my opinion, Mr. Speaker, unlikely to increase that representation at any future election. Yet 25 per cent of those casting votes in the province of Alberta in the last federal election voted for the Liberal party, and 19 per cent in the last federal election voted for the Progressive Conservatives in Quebec. The resulting number of seats gained from that vote distorts the real meaning of democracy. So in this House we have two large parties that are not really national at all, and two minor parties-the Credi-tistes with almost all of their support from Quebec, and the New Democratic Party which is made up of a few industrial seats in Ontario and British Columbia, and a small rump of agrarian radicals from the prairies.

speechtext:
There have been many, both inside and outside this House, who have said that the Senate should be resurrected-that is, if it ever was alive-so as to reflect the more regional points of view. One suggestion is that lists of nominees for Senate appointments be prepared by provincial governments. This, in my opinion, Mr. Speaker, would handcuff the administration of national affairs in Canada much as it has in France, the United States and Australia where bicameral legislatures exist. I believe it is essential for the efficient government of a country that there be one national decision-making body-in our case, parliament. However, I believe the method of election of members to parliament could be radically changed to reflect the true sentiments of the people of this country.
There have been many arguments over the years for a system of proportional representation in government. 1 believe that is perhaps the one answer to solving present Canadian problems. We have to overcome the dilemma of, in effect, having a one-party state as a result of an electoral system that creates a terrible bias by the "winner take all" theory in each constituency. West Germany could, perhaps, be used as a model for any mixed or proportional representation system.
I would put before the House the following suggestion. When the British North America Act is patriated, it should include structural change to the parliamentary system which would continue to allot seats to each province in proportion to population as we now have it, with the same constitutional guarantees that were made to Quebec and to Prince Edward Island, but stipulate that only half the seats in any particular province would be filled by direct election. The remaining 50 per cent of all members in each province would, as in West Germany, be elected by means of a preferential proportional voting system. For those who wish to pursue this idea in depth,
I would like to draw attention to the excellent summary of Geoffrey K. Roberts in his book entitled "West German Politics."
It is precisely because parliament does not accurately reflect the views of all parts of this country that regional frustrations have tended to be expressed by the provinces, and with this expression of regional frustrations the power of the provinces has grown inordinately, so that there is much duplication of government in addition to a tendency toward distortion of national fiscal policy by wanton provincial borrowing both from domestic and foreign sources. The notion of equal strength of provinces and the central government as expressed by the Leader of the Opposition and by the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) is contradictory. Any continuing devolution of federal powers, whether it be to Quebec or to Alberta, will fracture this country beyond repair, and in only a very few years. I urge and challenge the Leader of the Opposition to come to grips with patriation of the constitution, to put aside his parochial views and, if he can, try to think of

October 19, 1976
The Address-Mr. Collenette
the national perspective. This may be difficult to do, because the Leader of the Opposition often appears but a mere handmaiden of rabid provincial interests who pull strings from Edmonton.
Finally, I want to say something on the question of national unity, bilingualism and the encouragement of French immersion courses in English-speaking provinces.

Mr. Speaker, many English-speaking Canadians born in Canada forget too easily what a minority group is up against. Simply ask a newly-arrived immigrant in Toronto if it is easy to be accepted by the majority. Put the same question to some of our Jewish friends. The answer will be a loud No. New Canadians must suffer hardships by reason of their language and cultural differences; they face discrimination by reason of colour or religion.
Generally speaking, immigrants accept those hardships. They feel it is the price to be paid for acceptance in this country. But the same does not apply to French-speaking Canadians. They are more than a minority, they are part of a minority ranking as an equal partner in this Canadian nation. This is a hard fact of Canadian life, recognized by all parties in Parliament
-except the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) and his friends.
However, moderate Francophones who are the majority in Quebec must constantly fight on two fronts. They have to fight the separatists whose arguments appeal to the emotions of their fellow citizens. They also have to fight Anglophones who, imbued with a racial superiority complex, make little effort to acknowledge the French fact in their daily lives.
Recent developments have been helping the Parti Quebecois and the separatists.
The Official Languages Act is the mortar that binds this country together. Within its terms is enshrined the legal right of Canadians of both languages to be served in their own language by their national government throughout the country. Whenever possible, I feel it is the people's wish that the government provide that service. This was the crux of the air traffic control conflict. If safety and bilingualism are compatible, why deny the implementation of bilingualism in that sector?
A majority of citizens in my riding, and certainly in this country, react favourably to the linguistic and cultural dilemma faced by our French-speaking partners. Only those who are misinformed are unable to accept the inevitable, namely that our country is made up of two founding peoples with two official languages.
[English)
The initiation of French immersion courses in Ottawa, with significant federal financial assistance, has achieved a measure of success almost embarrassing to the government of Ontario, which has substantial jurisdiction over education. The success of this and other programs across the country probably

prompted Mr. Spicer to advocate increased bilingual education of young Canadians in Canadian schools.
Following Mr. Spicer's sensible recommendations, and in keeping with the sentiments expressed in the Speech from the Throne, I have a suggestion to make to the newly appointed Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) who, incidentally, is sitting in this House now. He will, I believe, make a tremendous contribution to national unity in his new office. When federal-provincial authorities this winter discuss the renewal of agreements whereby the federal government pays a share of postsecondary education, I believe the government should make, as a condition of its financial support, the requirement that those seeking entry to all university degree programs should be proficient in a second language. The second language need not necessarily be French or English; it could be Italian, Greek, Ukrainian or just about any second language.
This would encourage the children of new Canadians whose mother tongue is other than French or English to pursue their cultural heritage. At the same time, they would be credited with skill in another language for purposes of university entrance. The children of English-speaking parents would, I believe, opt almost exclusively for French as a second language, and children of French-speaking parents would opt almost exclusively for English studies.
I have noted in Toronto during the past few years, on the radio and the other media, expressions of hostility aimed at the Official Languages Act and the undeniable fact of this country's two founding languages and cultures; yet English-speaking parents, especially those in the largely defined middle-class, are among the first to demand French immersion courses in their children's schools. In metropolitan Toronto there are waiting lists of English-speaking students wanting to get into French immersion schools. It is noteworthy that the Ontario Minister of Education, Mr. Wells, recently said it was his aim and the aim of the government of Ontario to ensure that French immersion courses are offered by every school board in Ontario where there is a demand. That is certainly a start.
[ Translation]
The time has come for the moderate people, who are the majority in Canada, to come forward and speak the language of reason. This is not the time to remain silent.
Particularly for the Anglophones.
What is at stake is Canada as a nation. It is also the principles of justice and democracy which have served us so well for more than a century. For myself, I do not intend to remain silent.

It is my intention this afternoon to make some very specific remarks relating to our Canadian cattle industry. Before doing so, I hope it will be appropriate to make a few brief references to my home constituency of Medicine Hat. Approximately half the population of the federal constituency of Medicine Hat live in the city of that name and in the nearby industrial town of Redcliff. The mayor of Medicine Hat, Ted Grimm, recently announced a new population figure of 33,220, an increase of 17 per cent over the past two years. He said that in his opinion this rapid rate of growth had peaked and that the city was now in a consolidation phase of more modest growth.
At the same time, the mayor of Redcliff, Alf Dutton, can rightfully be proud of an annual population growth of 10 per cent over the past six years to a current total of 2,991 at the June census. These are satisfying growth figures. I should know, because after many years of no growth or, indeed, periods of population shrinkage, these figures are indeed satisfying to those of us in my constituency. They are mainly the result of our recent petrochemical and fertilizer development which is just now coming on stream.
The petrochemical industry is very important to the joint communities of Medicine Hat and Redcliff. The day after the throne speech was presented, Premier Lougheed of Alberta reminded all Canadians of this fact. In a brief reference in his state of the province speech, the premier made it very clear, and I quote:
Petrosar is a reality but one thing it won't be is an approved purchaser from the Alberta Petroleum Marketing Commission.
He also reminded us that this Alberta position was clearly spelled out on May 16, 1974. Last weekend, at our Quebec City caucus, 1 had a most interesting conversation with a Quebec lawyer on provincial resource development. We were generally agreed that Alberta and Quebec held somewhat similar views as to the development of non-renewable resources within our provincial boundaries. As I said, we were agreed on this. However, just as we parted company my Quebec friend said, as a very profound afterthought, "The only trouble is, you people in Alberta have too much."
It is not my intention today to make any apologies for my premier or my province. However, 1 do suggest that the rough justice of the 1930s on the prairies has finally been somewhat tempered two generations later. I also suggest that our at-home non-renewable resource development is necessary to compensate for the present-day transportation inequities. Our resources must be developed wisely. We in Alberta are very conscious of this and we will be ever mindful of the non-partisan wisdom all of us were privileged to hear last night from my
The Address-Mr. Hargrave
colleague, the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. MacLean). After all, land and its resources are not something you inherit from your parents; they are things you borrow from your children. We should never forget that.
During the summer recess, at various meetings, visits and travels in my constituency the topics of conversation raised by my constituents nearly always involved at least one or all of the following topics: the obvious bilingual issue, the international political footwork of the government during the Olympics, the capital punishment, peace and security package of legislation, and the government's controls policy. There were very few purely local issues raised with me, just these very serious national and international ones. It should come as no surprise to all members that there were the usual salty comments about the decline in popularity and credibility of the Trudeau government. Running through all these constituency chats was a distinct undercurrent of suspicion and distrust of the direction in which Canada is heading.
Finally, after four years, the left of centre emphasis on legislation that began in the two-year minority parliament is being seriously questioned, if only because of the staggering costs that are now so apparent, surely, to all Canadians. Yesterday's by-elections' results must surely be the final proof, if any were needed, of this personal assessment.
I now wish to turn to agricultural matters and to the Canadian beef cattle industry in particular. No Speech from the Throne in recent memory contained less reference to agriculture than the one now under debate. Only 42 words were used to discuss strictly farm matters. It seems "consultations" are finally to be held with the provinces and farm organizations to "strengthen the structure and productivity of Canadian agriculture". Surely the major disappointment must be that Canada's beef cattle crisis was completely ignored, and this in the face of continuous and massive offshore beef imports and another pending beef war with the United States triggered by President Ford's beef quota announcement on October 9.
Let us examine our current cattle situation. The two major components of our cattle industry, cow-calf and the feeding sectors, continue to be seriously depressed with market prices well below actual costs of production. Fat steers have been losing from $50 to $125 per head since early spring. The same situation generally holds true in the U.S.A. An expected upturn in fed cattle prices in both countries did not develop because of three factors-abnormally high steer numbers in the beef pipeline, the excessive level of beef imports from Australia and New Zealand, and continuing high domestic feed grain prices which contribute so much to sustained high costs of feed lot gains.
The North American beef cattle industry is in serious trouble, essentially because we have too many cattle, especially cows and steers. There is only one outlet for this abnormal production-consumers in the United States and Canada. The cost of moving surplus beef offshore is prohibitive and only

October 19, 1976
The Address-Mr. Hargrave
accentuates the truth of the fact that no other country in the world can afford to buy North American cattle or beef even at today's depressed producer prices. We must continue, literally, to eat our own surplus on this continent. I must add that we are doing a pretty good job of this. Canada's beef consumption, per capita, is up by five pounds compared to the same period last year.
After a seven-year build-up in cow numbers-43 per cent for beef cows-our national breeding herd began to decline in the fall and winter of last year. But last year's record high calf crop is still in the beef pipeline. Cow numbers will continue to decline this fall and winter, but there is no indication of any shortage of breeding cattle or, of course, feeder cattle. Last August, the U.S. Beef Industry Council summed up the whole situation very succinctly by saying:
Everything comes down to having 10 per cent to 11 per cent more beef production this year than last... we have to work extra hard to move this large supply.
There are two issues currently before our Canadian cattle industry. Each is highly political and their successful resolution is indispensable if the present cattle crisis is to end. First, there are the offshore beef imports from Australia and New Zealand. I consider this issue to be the most important one in the short term. Second, there is the Canada-U.S. cattle and beef trade which I consider to be more important in the area of long-term policy determination.
While these two issues have an obvious common denominator-cattle-they are separate and distinct and must be discussed separately. With regard to the offshore imports issue I would say this: in the face of current record high supplies of North American beef, the last thing we need is a massive increase in imports of beef from "down under." Accumulated imports for the first nine months of 1976 are now up by approximately 55 per cent over the same time-frame in 1975. Some 145,118,000 pounds of frozen carcass and boneless beef entered Canada as of the week ending October 2, 1976, an increase of about 50.9 million pounds compared with 1975.
With the unlimited access to our markets presently enjoyed by Australia and New-Zealand, year-end totals will make up approximately 10 per cent or 11 per cent of total Canadian beef consumption. Further complicating this issue, such imports have been priced 15 cents to 25 cents per pound below the prices of equivalent imports into the U.S. markets and right now they are still coming in up to 15 cents below those prices in spite of the one-sided "six cents under" rule agreed to by Canada on June 11 last.
Why should a pound of Australian or New Zealand beef be worth less than a pound of Canadian beef? This so-called "six cents under" rule was a sell-out by our Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and its minister at the time. Apparently, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) was a party to the deal.
My questions in the House on July 7 and July 8 stated the cattlemen's position in no uncertain terms, and the former minister of industry, trade and commerce said he would take them as notice "to find out the basis of the conclusion which

was drawn". Of course, the minister never did respond in the House to the questions I raised. On July 16, in anticipation of this lack of action, I wrote a personal letter to the minister asking for a proper explanation. Two months later he did respond in the course of a lengthy letter which sought to justify the "six cents under" rule. He said, in part:
During recent years the Canadian boneless beef market has been based on an export equivalent, a term with which you, as a cattleman, are familiar. The price for boneless beef and cows in Canada has been determined by the level at which boneless beef, cows, or both, could be sold in the United States.
I am indeed familar with the term "export equivalent", but I am amazed that the minister's senior staff would be so naive as to advise him that Canadian market levels are always at this export equivalent. Our boneless beef market is determined by the dominant U.S. market, but in actual practice it floats between a Canadian export floor and a U.S. import ceiling. Our minimum boneless beef price will be the United States price less tariff, less freight, less other expenses, plus or minus the dollar exchange. Our maximum price would be the United States price plus tariff, plus freight and other expenses, plus or minus the dollar exchange. This means, of course, that depending on the relative domestic supply situation in each country, our prices can be above or below United States prices.
There is no reason that Canada should always operate at the export floor level. The "six cents under" rule simply means that Canadian producers are paying the tariff and transportation charges on equivalent volumes of Australian and New Zealand beef imports. This is a considerable amount of money. Hon. members may be familar with the current round of questions in the House on this issue.
In spite of the statement by the Minister of Agriculture as reported at page 103 of Hansard of October 15, that no beef or veal would be allowed into Canada after Sunday night, October 17, unless by permit, one fact remains clear: nowhere has the minister stated he intends to restrict, reduce or, hopefully, temporarily stop Australian and New Zealand beef imports into Canada. The minister's individual permit device is merely a diversion which indicates no intention whatever of "federal action to protect beef markets", to quote the heading of his news release of October 13.
The Canadian cattle and beef market continues to remain the only major market in the world without protection against offshore imports. United States cattle producers have their meat import law and we saw how effective it was last October 9. The minister refuses to consider the counterpart of that, a Canadian meat import law; he says that our Export and Import Permits Act will accomplish the same results. But nowhere has he acted to use this legislation that is presently on the books. I say to this House that it is completely irresponsible for the Minister of Agriculture to suggest that these imports do not compete with our fed cattle markets. He has said this consistently all through the summer.
While our frozen carcass imports generally supplement our domestic cow-beef supplies, these frozen, boneless cuts do compete directly with our grade A fresh beef supplies. Witness
October 19, 1976

last week's sudden market strength in the United States that was due mainly to a sympathetic reaction by U.S. cattlemen and the entire industry to their prompt quota action on offshore imports. The same market increases could occur here if similar action were taken with respect to offshore imports of beef.
Before leaving this item, Mr. Speaker, it should be pointed out that in 1975 Canada had a deficit trade balance with Australia and New Zealand of some $113,034,000. Historically, Canada has been a net exporter in its trade with these two countries until the last few years. Our main export commodities to Australia and New Zealand are manufactured products. It now seems highly probable that the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is deliberately using this trade deficit as a trading lever for further manufactured goods in our trade with these two countries-at the expense, of course, of our Canadian cattle industry.
I should now like to deal with the second major cattle issue, the Canadian-United States cattle and beef trade. As I intimated earlier, this is the more important in terms of long-term policy development for Canada's cattle industry. Recent developments in our cattle and beef dealings with the United States have become headline items, starting with the firing of United States Secretary Earl Butz and the subsequent imposition of meat import quotas by the United States. This, of course, is recognized as a highly political issue in that country, with both parties trying to attract the farm vote in the final stages of their election campaigns.
Let me take a quick lodk at the cattle and beef trade with our trading partner, the United States. The following figures are from the Department of Agriculture's blue book of statistics on livestock marketing, and they are for the last week of record, October 2, 1976. These are the cumulative totals from January 1 to October 2, 1976, a period of some nine months. Canada's imports of beef amount now to 17.8 million pounds; one year ago the corresponding figure was 9.4 million. As for imports of slaughter cattle, which includes both cattle and slaughter calves, imports amounted to 147,804 head; last year the corresponding figure was 65,653 head.
Now the other side of the coin, our exports to the United States. We exported 71.8 million pounds of beef, compared with only 14.5 million pounds last year. As for cattle, which includes four categories, slaughter cattle, feeders, beef breeding cattle and slaughter calves, we exported 231,936 head this year, compared with 34,065 head in 1975. It is of interest to note that during the last week of record, ending October 2, 5,837 head of slaughter cattle and calves were imported into Canada. I repeat, that was in one week, Mr. Speaker. Most of these cattle came into either Ontario or Manitoba. The point is that right now, in spite of heavy imports of United States fed cattle, in our total trade balance with the United States we have a substantial positive trade balance in dollars, number of head and pounds of beef. We should not forget that at the negotiating table with the U.S.A.
Several weeks ago our agricultural minister made some statements on CBC radio concerning offshore imports. He
The Address-Mr. Hargrave
took the occasion to sort of brag about this healthy Canadian trade balance with the United States. Surely, in view of recent developments, this was not a very prudent thing to do-to rub it in, if you like, or to flaunt it in the face of United States cattlemen and politicians in the heat of their presidential campaign. Canada cannot afford even remotely to consider another cattle and beef war with the United States. Our memories cannot be that short.
While I have always strongly supported the concept that we must remain a vital part of the North American cattle and beef market, I quickly add that this concept must be fair both ways. Right now, the United States meat import law and their 10 per cent ad valorem duty on our processed meat exports gives a clear advantage to the United States at the negotiating table. 1 suggest that Canada's cattle industry is much better off in the North American market, even if we have to negotiate these unfair items, than risking the total loss of the United States market which must be considered inevitable if our cattle industry moves in a supply-management direction. Let us not forget, Mr. Speaker, the 100,000 Canadian cows that were absorbed by the United States market in 1975, or what they would have been worth in Canada without that market.
Yesterday afternoon unofficial United States sources suggested that our U.S. quota will be 80.4 million pounds of beef for the whole of calendar year 1976. I stress that this figure comes from an unofficial United States source. This, of course, is considerably short of the minister's figure of 90 million pounds. With the actual figure now approaching 74 million pounds as of today, it becomes more important than ever that Canada act immediately to restrict Australian and New Zealand imports before our own surplus starts to back up when the United States quota is filled, perhaps early in November.
I have been somewhat critical, Mr. Speaker, of the government's direction, or lack of it, in our cattle industry, particularly under the agriculture and industry, trade and commerce ministers. I trust that the members of this House will recognize that these are truly objective comments, even if it is the way I see it.
In concluding these throne speech remarks, I wish to record, again as I see it, three short-term policy recommendations and four long-term policy considerations relating to our beef cattle industry. I shall deal first with the short-term items. First, there should be immediate and even retroactive action on the Australian-New Zealand meat import issue by the establishment of a Canadian meat import law or by making the import permits act really work. Second, if federal political action is necessary at the producer level, let it be limited to a stop-loss stabilization approach as provided for by the minister's own Bill C-50, but not a top-loaded plan.
Third, let those provinces already operating their own programs-they are British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec-continue until a federal stoploss policy becomes operative. You must remember that a number of these provincial plans are based on individual
230

October 19, 1976
The Address-Mr. Hargrave
five-year contracts, so it would be extremely difficult to superimpose a federal program on them. At the same time, and in addition to the last item, let us have an announcement now as to what the fed cattle support price is for 1976. Surely this is long overdue; it has been promised by the minister practically throughout the year.
Let me turn to long-term cattle policy considerations. First, we should not be recommending supply-management for Canada's beef cattle industry. If this development ever comes into being, it must be as a result of a request by Canada's beef producers only, and not by federal government promotion. Second, we should strive to preserve the North American market concept that recognizes the two-way flow of both live cattle and beef with nominal tariffs only between Canada and the United States. Third, we should recognize and eliminate the east-west inequities that currently exist-I am thinking here of transportation costs-resulting in a gradual but definite shift in Canada's feeding industry for cattle and hogs from western Canada to Ontario and Quebec.
Fourth, we should decide now that Canada can, and should, go all out to produce cattle and beef in vigorous competition with the United States, even if it means moving to a net export position. I am sure that is the position we now have in Canada. Finally, Mr. Speaker, surely our Canadian cattle industry has had far too many ill-advised, short-term, ad hoc government policies, both federal and provincial, with absolutely no clearly defined long-term policy objectives. The single exception here, of course, is the obsession of the Minister of Agriculture in respect of supply management for our cattle industry. This is an approach which I cannot accept. Surely the time is overdue for politicians to think and plan in terms of the next generation of cattle producers, rather than in terms of the next election. Promises of federal subsidies might win a few votes and lose our cattle industry.
